title: Reaction types and balancing equations
blurb: Count atoms in formulas, balance equations with coefficients, classify the six reaction types and spot oxidation and reduction.
question: A study guide shows CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O and asks you to balance it, name the reaction type and say which substance is oxidized. Where do you start?

teach.body: Formally, a chemical equation shows reactants (left) turning into products (right), with formulas, coefficients and states: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. In plain English: it is a recipe card. Subscripts tell you the atoms in one molecule (H₂O = 2 H, 1 O). Coefficients tell you how many molecules (3 H₂O = 6 H, 3 O). A subscript outside parentheses multiplies everything inside.

head: Written
Atoms counted
teach.caption: Coefficient × subscript gives the atom count. With parentheses, multiply the subscript outside by each atom inside.

teach.h: Conservation of mass: balance with coefficients
teach.body: The law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier): atoms are rearranged in a reaction, never created or destroyed, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products and each kind of atom appears in equal numbers on both sides. Balance an equation by changing coefficients only. Never change a subscript: that would turn the substance into something else (H₂O into H₂O₂).

steps.label: Count
steps.sub: Left: 1 C, 4 H, 2 O. Right: 1 C, 2 H, 3 O

steps.label: Hydrogen
steps.sub: Put 2 before H₂O: now 4 H each side

steps.label: Oxygen
steps.sub: Right has 2 + 2 = 4 O; put 2 before O₂

teach.caption: Balance elements that appear in only one formula per side first; leave free elements like O₂ until last.

head: Type
Pattern
Example
teach.caption: Neutralization is a type of double replacement. A double replacement often forms a precipitate, such as solid AgCl.

teach.body: Oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons. They always happen together in a redox reaction: whatever one substance loses, another gains. In 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl, sodium is oxidized (loses an electron) and chlorine is reduced (gains it). Rusting, combustion and cellular respiration are all redox reactions.

teach.caption: Another version: LEO the lion says GER (Lose Electrons Oxidation, Gain Electrons Reduction).

items.label: molar mass of H₂O: sum of its atomic masses

teach.caption: Coefficients can be read as moles: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O means 2 mol of hydrogen react with 1 mol of oxygen.

teach.body: Carlos, a pre-nursing student, checks that C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O is balanced. Carbon: 6 = 6. Hydrogen: 12 = 6 × 2 = 12. Oxygen: left 6 + (6 × 2) = 18; right (6 × 2) + 6 = 18. Every atom matches, so mass is conserved. Glucose is oxidized to CO₂ while oxygen is reduced to water, so this is also a redox reaction.

teach.text: Never balance by changing subscripts. AB + CD → AD + CB is DOUBLE replacement (two compounds swap partners), not single. Combustion products are CO₂ and H₂O, never O₂. And when a gas escapes an open container, mass is not destroyed: the gas carries it away.

items: Subscripts count atoms in a molecule; coefficients count molecules. 2 Ca(OH)₂ = 2 Ca, 4 O, 4 H.
Mass is conserved: equal numbers of each atom on both sides. Balance with coefficients only.
Synthesis A + B → AB; decomposition AB → A + B; single A + BC → AC + B; double AB + CD → AD + CB.
Combustion: fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water.
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons; they always occur together.

summary: You can now count atoms in any formula, balance equations using coefficients and explain why mass is conserved. You can also classify synthesis, decomposition, single and double replacement, combustion and neutralization reactions and identify what is oxidized and reduced.

A.q: Which type of reaction is Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂?
A.why: An element (Zn) replaces another element (H) in a compound: A + BC → AC + B.

whyNot.0: Synthesis combines reactants into one product; here there are two products.
whyNot.2: Double replacement needs two compounds swapping partners; zinc is a lone element.
whyNot.3: Decomposition starts with a single compound breaking apart.

A.q: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 2 Ca(OH)₂?
A.why: Each Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O (the subscript 2 multiplies OH). Two formula units give 2 × 2 = 4 O.

whyNot.0: 2 counts the oxygen in only one Ca(OH)₂ and ignores the coefficient.
whyNot.1: 8 multiplies the coefficient, the subscript and an extra 2; the correct count is 2 × 2.
whyNot.2: 10 is the total of all atoms (2 Ca + 4 O + 4 H), not just oxygen.

A.q: Which type of reaction is AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃?
A.why: Two compounds swap partners (AB + CD → AD + CB), forming a precipitate of AgCl.

whyNot.1: Single replacement involves a lone element replacing one in a compound; both reactants here are compounds.
whyNot.2: Synthesis forms one product; here there are two.
whyNot.3: Combustion needs a fuel reacting with O₂ to make CO₂ and H₂O.

B.q: Which coefficients balance N₂ + __ H₂ → __ NH₃?

whyNot.0: With 1 NH₃ the right has 1 N but the left has 2.
whyNot.1: 2 H₂ gives 4 H, while 3 NH₃ gives 9 H and 3 N.
whyNot.3: 3 NH₃ gives 3 N, but the left has only 2 N.

B.q: A student heats 5.0 g of magnesium ribbon in an open dish. The white powder left weighs more than 5.0 g. What is the best explanation?
options: It combined with oxygen from air
The heat converted into extra mass
Its atoms each gained extra neutrons
Ash from the dish was added to it
B.why: Magnesium combines with oxygen from the air (a synthesis). The product's mass includes that oxygen, so mass is conserved overall.

whyNot.1: Heat does not create mass; conservation of mass holds in chemical reactions.
whyNot.2: Chemical reactions involve electrons only; nuclei and neutrons are unchanged.
whyNot.3: The dish does not react; the extra mass is the oxygen that combined with the metal.

B.q: In the reaction 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl, sodium is:
B.why: Sodium loses one electron to become Na⁺. Loss of electrons is oxidation (OIL RIG).

whyNot.0: Gaining electrons is reduction, and that happens to chlorine, not sodium.
whyNot.1: Losing electrons is oxidation, not reduction.
whyNot.2: Sodium loses its valence electron; it does not gain one.

C.why: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: 1 Ca, 1 C and 3 O on each side.

whyNot.0: The left has 2 O and the right has 1; it needs 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
whyNot.1: The right has 4 O but the left has 2; it needs 2 O₂.
whyNot.2: The left has 4 H and 4 O; the right has 2 H and 3 O. It needs 2 H₂O on the right.

C.q: To balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, a student rewrites it as H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂. What is wrong with this?
options: It is acceptable, since the atoms now match
Changing a subscript changed the product
A coefficient of 2 should go in front of O₂
Hydrogen gas should be written as single H
C.why: Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ makes hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Balance with coefficients: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.

whyNot.0: The atoms match, but the product is now the wrong substance; subscripts must not be changed.
whyNot.2: 2 O₂ would give 4 O on the left; the fix is coefficients of 2 before H₂ and H₂O.
whyNot.3: Hydrogen is diatomic and is correctly written H₂.

C.q: In the balanced equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, how many oxygen atoms are on each side?

whyNot.0: 12 counts only the O₂ molecules on the left and misses glucose's 6 oxygens.
whyNot.1: 6 counts only the oxygen in one glucose molecule.
whyNot.3: 24 double-counts; each side totals 18 oxygen atoms.

reteach.title: Partners on the dance floor
reteach.question: Picture couples at a dance. How do pairing up, breaking up, cutting in and swapping partners match the reaction types?

blocks.body: Synthesis: two single dancers pair up (A + B → AB). Decomposition: a couple splits (AB → A + B). Single replacement: a solo dancer cuts in and takes one partner, leaving the other alone (A + BC → AC + B). Double replacement: two couples swap partners (AB + CD → AD + CB). Nobody enters or leaves the hall, which is conservation of mass: you can add more identical couples (coefficients), but you cannot change who a couple is made of (subscripts).

blocks.text: If there is a lone element on the left, think 'cutting in' (single). If two compounds trade, think 'swap' (double).

explain.body: Subscripts count atoms within one molecule; a subscript after parentheses multiplies everything inside. Coefficients multiply the whole formula. Total atoms = coefficient × subscript.

test.q: How many hydrogen atoms are represented by 3 H₂O?
test.why: Each H₂O has 2 H; 3 molecules have 3 × 2 = 6 H.

whyNot.1: 2 is the hydrogen count in one molecule and ignores the coefficient.
whyNot.2: 3 is the number of molecules, not the number of hydrogen atoms.
whyNot.3: 5 adds the coefficient and subscript; they must be multiplied.

explain.body: Count each atom on both sides. Adjust coefficients until every element matches. Never change subscripts, which would change the substance. Mass is conserved because atoms are only rearranged.

test.q: When balancing a chemical equation, what are you allowed to change?
test.why: Only coefficients change; they set how many of each molecule take part.

whyNot.0: Changing subscripts changes the identity of the substance.
whyNot.1: The products are fixed by the reaction; rewriting them describes a different reaction.
whyNot.3: The reactants are also fixed; you can only change how many of each are used.

explain.body: Synthesis (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), single replacement (A + BC → AC + B), double replacement (AB + CD → AD + CB), combustion (fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O) and neutralization (acid + base → salt + water).

test.q: Which type of reaction is CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O?
test.why: A hydrocarbon fuel reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water: combustion.

whyNot.0: Synthesis produces a single product; this reaction has two.
whyNot.2: Decomposition starts from one compound breaking apart; here methane reacts with oxygen.
whyNot.3: Double replacement swaps partners between two compounds; O₂ is an element, and the CO₂ + H₂O pattern marks combustion.

explain.body: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. One cannot happen without the other. Rusting, combustion and cellular respiration are redox reactions.

test.q: Which statement about oxidation and reduction is correct?
options: Oxidation is a gain of electrons
Reduction is a loss of electrons
Oxidation can take place without reduction
test.why: Electrons lost by one substance must be gained by another, so oxidation and reduction always occur together.

whyNot.0: Oxidation is a LOSS of electrons (OIL).
whyNot.1: Reduction is a GAIN of electrons (RIG).
whyNot.2: Lost electrons must go somewhere, so reduction accompanies every oxidation.
